prose: As developers increasingly ship code they did not write or fully review, this essay argues the bottleneck has moved from writing code to verifying it. It cites a 2026 Faros study of 22,000 developers across 4,000 teams: throughput rises with AI adoption, but bugs, rework, review load and incidents rise faster - 54% more bugs per developer, a fivefold increase in median PR review time, and over three times as many incidents per PR. The author stresses these are correlations, and a later Q3 report showed some effects easing while downstream verification and remediation costs kept piling up.

The proposed answer is automated software verification: at the speed AI generates diffs, no small team can meaningfully review them, so correctness has to be established by tooling rather than human reading alone.
highlights: Faros 2026 study: 22,000 developers, 4,000 teams, two years of telemetry
High AI adoption correlates with 54% more bugs per developer
Median PR review time up roughly fivefold; incidents per PR up 3x
Author cautions these are correlations, not proof of cause
Argues human review cannot scale to AI-generated diffs
Proposes automated software verification as the path to keep speed without losing quality
